extracted.intended_audience: mathematical students and practitioners (readers of a 19th-century mathematical periodical)
extracted.subtask_description: A collection of classical mathematical constructions, theorems, and algorithmic methods (geometry, analysis, algebra, and trigonometry) with worked demonstrations and corollaries intended for student study and problem solving.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of a rectilineal figure approximately equal to the area of a given circle (Prop. V)
rubrics_metrics.description: A straight-edge construction (divide a line into three equal parts, erect perpendiculars, form points C,D,E,F,G,H, draw lines MN, KL, diagonals MK, LN, construct circle with centre O radius OB) producing a rectilineal figure MLKN asserted to be equal (approximately) in area to the circle of radius OB.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives step-by-step construction instructions (divide AB into three equal parts AF,FE,EB; construct CD at right angle; make CE = AE, ED = EB; join C and F; cut off FG = FE; draw EH from E; draw MN through C and H; drop perpendiculars from A and B meeting MN at M and N; draw KL parallel to MN through D; intersect ML and NK at L and K; form diagonals MK and LN intersecting at O; with center O and radius OB draw circle BHAD). Notes: no original demonstration accompanied the construction; the contributor later showed the construction is only approximately true and that MLKN is actually greater than the circle (analysis/series expressions given). Historical/context note: probably derived from an Indian (Hindoo) quadrature attempt; useful as an example of approximate geometric quadrature. Use caution: the construction is approximate, not exact quadrature; the author provides algebraic evidence showing the discrepancy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shell attraction problems → admissible laws of attraction
rubrics_metrics.description: Analysis of the gravitational/electrical attraction of a homogeneous spherical shell upon internal and external points: by integrating the elemental attractions and imposing that (i) the attraction on an external point equals that of the entire mass concentrated at the centre, and (ii) the attraction on an internal point is zero, deduce constraints on the radial law of attraction f(r).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sets up integral expressions for total attraction using geometry (angles, element positions) and unknown radial law f; derives functional/differential equations by requiring the shell theorem conditions to hold for all radii and distances; expands in powers and equates coefficients to determine admissible forms. Conclusion: the admissible laws are those combining inverse powers, but the only law that satisfies both shell-theorem conditions in general is inverse-square (p ∝ 1/r^2); sign distinctions for repulsion noted. Method guidance: form integral, eliminate angular variable, compare with 4πu^2 f(7) (attraction as if concentrated at centre), differentiate with respect to shell radius, expand in power series, equate coefficients and solve for functional form; interpret physical consequences (e.g., free surface charge collects on sphere, implying inverse-square electrical repulsion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Analytical theorem relating area of triangle formed by perpendicular feet to original triangle (Simson-like area relation)
rubrics_metrics.description: If from any point P in the plane of triangle ABC perpendiculars are dropped to the three sides and the feet are joined pairwise to form triangle QRS (denoted A'), then A' is related to the original triangle area A, the circumradius R, and the distance R' from P to the circumcenter by a specific formula; the relation differs depending on whether P is inside or outside the circumcircle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper gives a full analytic derivation: denote O circumcenter, OD,OE,OF perpendicular bisectors; express PQ,PR,PS in terms of R and R' and an angle parameter a; compute 2A' via PQ·PR·sin C + ...; after algebraic reduction the expression for twice the area of QRS becomes 2A' = 2A + (expression involving R' and sin A sin B sin C). Using a cited identity (Art. XXIX cor. 8), substitution simplifies the relation and yields the final formula which distinguishes the 'within' and 'without' circumcircle cases. Guidance for use: apply when studying Simson line properties or area transforms under perpendicular projections; corollaries include scaling under equal-angle oblique drops and special cases when P lies on the concentric circle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simson line (feet of perpendiculars collinear when point on circumcircle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Application of the previous theorem: when the chosen point P lies on the circumcircle of triangle ABC, the triangle formed by the feet of perpendiculars collapses (A' vanishes) and the feet are collinear — the classical Simson line result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derives directly from the general area relation by setting the appropriate radius/distance values so that A' = 0; the paper remarks this yields the well-known result 'If from any point in the circumference of the circumcircle, perpendiculars be let fall upon the sides, then the feet are in the same straight line.' Also cross-references synthetic proofs in other works; useful as an analytic proof route and as an exercise for students to recover a synthetic demonstration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jacobi's theorem on four perpendiculars collinearity (extension of Simson line)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given triangle ABC, let AD,BE,CF be altitudes from vertices. From the extremity of one altitude (say the foot E_k of one altitude) draw perpendiculars to the other two altitudes and to the other two sides; the four resulting perpendicular-foot points are collinear and the line is parallel to the line joining the extremities of the other two altitudes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof given by constructing circles through appropriate triples (e.g., circle through E,H,C,B) and applying the previous perpendicular-to-side collinearity property (Simson-like) on those triangles. The exposition notes the method's elegance and suggests a synthetic geometric proof would be desirable as a student exercise. Use: demonstrates technique of reducing new collinearity claims to previously established Simson/circle-perpendicular facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Horner's synthetic division — algorithmic rule and elementary proof
rubrics_metrics.description: A didactic statement and proof of Horner's method (synthetic division) for dividing polynomials (and for evaluating series expansions) expressed as an algorithm using vertical columns and oblique columns of coefficients; enumerated procedural steps (a)–(m) give the practical rule for computing quotient coefficients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stepwise rule: (a) write dividend coefficients horizontally; (b) set divisor's coefficients (with sign changes except leading 1) in a vertical column to left; (c) draw equality line; (d) bring down first dividend coefficient as first quotient coefficient; (e) multiply vertical divisor coefficients (except leading 1) by first quotient coefficient to form first oblique column, shifted right; (f) add second column to get second quotient coefficient; (g) repeat to obtain subsequent quotient coefficients until termination or required order. Proof strategy: view the tabular arrangement as an arithmetical equality of columns; transpose oblique columns to other side (changing signs) to show the tabular result is algebraically identical to polynomial multiplication; therefore procedure yields correct quotient coefficients. Guidance & uses: recommended for elementary study; useful for series development, numerical root-finding, factorial transforms, recurring series; notes on bookkeeping: supply zeros for missing terms, keep signs, and understand the vertical/oblique interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Straight line of quickest descent to a curve (rectilinear brachistochrone for straight-line path)
rubrics_metrics.description: For the problem of finding the straight line of quickest descent from a given point to a given curve in the same vertical plane, the required straight line always bisects the angle between the normal to the curve at the meeting point and the vertical ordinate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set up the travel-time functional L (proportional to arc length/time under gravity representation), express L in coordinates, and minimize L by calculus to derive the Euler-type condition. After algebraic manipulation the extremal condition reduces to the geometric statement that the required straight line bisects the angle between the curve's normal at the contact point and the vertical line through that contact. Practical use: reduces the search for the optimal contact point to solving the algebraic condition obtained after substituting the bisector relation together with the curve equation; if one of the two lines is vertical this reduces to a simpler relation. This provides a geometric characterization to guide computations and constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: General theorem and corollaries on properties of the parabola (parabolic segment relations)
rubrics_metrics.description: A general theorem relating the sums of parabolic segments cut off by chords of an inscribed polygon to certain expressions in the chord endpoints' coordinates; followed by many corollaries: (1) parabolic segment equals two-thirds of associated tangent triangle, (2) relations among tangent-formed triangles (ratios and products), (3) constancy/product-equalities for tangent contact sets, (4) equal partitioning of a parabolic segment by lines parallel to axis, (5) formulas for polygons inscribed in a parabola with equal segments, and numerical relations expressing areas of rectilinear figures formed by joining points on the parabola.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The theorem is proved by coordinate integration using axis through vertex and tangent at vertex; explicit formulas for a typical parabolic segment and summation produce the main identity. Corollaries illustrated: how parabolic segments relate to triangles bounded by tangents (2/3 rule), special algebraic identities among areas of tangent-formed triangles, equal-segment partition properties (divide chord into equal parts and draw parallels → equal parabolic segments), and combinatorial area formulas for inscribed polygons (expressed in terms of n, m etc.). Use: this cluster supplies many standard results about parabolas useful for problem solving in classical analytic geometry and for generating exercises; students can apply coordinate methods and use the 2/3 segment-triangle property repeatedly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transformation of algebraic equations using auxiliary symmetric functions
rubrics_metrics.description: A method of transforming algebraic equations (quadratic, cubic, biquadratic, etc.) to simpler forms (e.g., binomial or reduced forms) by forming auxiliary expressions v built from symmetric functions of the roots (using roots of unity), deriving a set of subsidiary equations ¢_i(v)=0, and choosing v (and parameters) so as to annihilate intermediate terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Framework: let given equation have symmetric coefficient functions p_i; form expressions ¢_i(v) by combining root powers with roots of unity; analyze conditions ¢_i(v)=0 and multiply/substitute to obtain a reducing equation for v. For each degree: quadratics — simple choices for v yield reduction; cubics — simultaneous conditions lead to a quadratic in the parameter to determine v; biquadratics — more stringent relations (extra equations) arise and one cannot always annihilate three middle terms simultaneously except under restrictive relations among coefficients. The paper gives explicit sample substitutions (e.g., take v = A x^m + a^'), examples of resulting reducing equations, and discusses when reductions are possible or impossible (e.g., necessity of relations like 3p1^2 = 8p2 in some contexts). Use: a uniform algebraico-symmetric approach to equation reduction; guidance to choose auxiliary v forms and to check necessary coefficient relations; references to earlier work by Hamilton, Jerrard, and others. Practical caution: changing the form of the auxiliary equation changes which reductions are possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derivation of fundamental trigonometric addition formulas via spherical-triangle limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Derives the cosine and sine addition/subtraction formulas (cos(a±b), sin(a±b)) from the fundamental spherical-triangle cosine formulas by letting one spherical angle tend to 0 or 180°, thereby recovering plane trigonometric addition identities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start from spherical-triangle relations cos a = cos b cos c + sin b sin c cos A, etc., then consider degenerate limits A→0 (one arc coincides) or A→180° (other degeneracy) to obtain cos(a−b) and cos(a+b) formulas. Combine with analogous limits of the other spherical relations to obtain sin(a±b) identities. Methodological note: the derivation emphasizes independence from pre-assumed plane trigonometric identities, grounding the addition formulas in spherical geometry and continuity arguments. Useful pedagogically as an alternative derivation rooted in geometric limits rather than algebraic manipulation alone.
